Public-domain source text — Robert Frost, An Old Man's Winter Night, Mountain Interval (New York: Henry Holt, 1916)
An Old Man's Winter Night
by Robert Frost
The following poem is by Robert Frost (1916).

```passage
All out of doors looked darkly in at him
Through the thin frost, almost in separate stars,
That gathers on the pane in empty rooms.
What kept his eyes from giving back the gaze
Was the lamp tilted near them in his hand.
What kept him from remembering what it was
That brought him to that creaking room was age.
He stood with barrels round him--at a loss.
And having scared the cellar under him
In clomping there, he scared it once again
In clomping off;--and scared the outer night,
Which has its sounds, familiar, like the roar
Of trees and crack of branches, common things,
But nothing so like beating on a box.
A light he was to no one but himself
Where now he sat, concerned with he knew what,
A quiet light, and then not even that.
He consigned to the moon, such as she was,
So late-arising, to the broken moon
As better than the sun in any case
For such a charge, his snow upon the roof,
His icicles along the wall to keep;
And slept. The log that shifted with a jolt
Once in the stove, disturbed him and he shifted,
And eased his heavy breathing, but still slept.
One aged man--one man--can't fill a house,
A farm, a countryside, or if he can,
It's thus he does it of a winter night.
```

The following poem is "An Old Man's Winter Night" by Robert Frost (1916). In this poem, the speaker describes an elderly man alone in his farmhouse on a winter night, following him from his confused visit to the cellar to his falling asleep by the stove while the dark, cold world presses in around the house.

Read the poem closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Robert Frost uses poetic elements and techniques to convey a complex view of the old man's solitude, in which his frailty, forgetfulness, and smallness against the vast winter night exist alongside a quiet, almost stubborn claim that his lone presence still keeps and fills the place.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the poem.
- Use specific evidence from the poem, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple poetic elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
Frost's old man is easy to pity. He forgets why he went to the cellar, he cannot meet the stare of the night, and by the end even his lamp is gone. But the poem does not let pity have the last word. Through personification, tangled syntax, and shrinking repetition, Frost shows a man reduced almost to nothing. Yet through possessive language and a final hedged statement, he insists that this reduced man still holds his house against the dark, and that holding it this way, half-asleep and barely visible, may be the only way anyone could.

The opening makes the man an object instead of an observer. "All out of doors looked darkly in at him" turns the whole winter world into a watcher, and the lamp "tilted near" his eyes keeps him from "giving back the gaze." The light that should help him see actually blinds him to what is outside, so from the first lines his one defense against the dark is also what isolates him. Frost then lets the sentence structure act out his confusion. "What kept him from remembering what it was" circles through two "what" clauses before it finally lands on "age," so the reader, like the man, has to grope for the point. When the line arrives at "at a loss," the dash before it works like a stall in his thinking, a blank where his purpose should be.

What makes this more than a portrait of decline is the speaker's dry humor. The man "scared the cellar under him / In clomping there," then scared it "once again" on the way out. "Clomping" is a clumsy, almost cartoonish word, and frightening a cellar is funny. But the joke turns when he scares "the outer night" too. The night knows the "roar / Of trees and crack of branches, common things," yet has heard nothing "so like beating on a box." The simile deflates him and is oddly proud of him at once: his noise is a hollow knocking, but it is also unlike anything in nature. For a moment the vast night is the one startled. Frost lets us laugh at the man without mocking him, because the small noise really does register.

The middle of the poem shrinks him through repetition. "A light he was to no one but himself" already narrows his reach, and "A quiet light, and then not even that" erases it. The word "light" dims every time it comes back. Read alone, this sounds like death, and the poem seems to lean that way. But Frost pulls back: the man "slept," shifts when a log jolts in the stove, and "still slept." "Still" means both motionless and continuing, so the poem gestures toward death while keeping him alive.

Even asleep, he claims ownership. He hands "his snow upon the roof, / His icicles along the wall" to the moon to keep. The possessives are stubborn, since snow and ice belong to no one, yet he treats them as property under his watch. His chosen keeper is "the broken moon," late and partial, "As better than the sun." A broken guardian fits a broken man, and his choice suggests he understands that diminished things can still do a job.

The last three lines rescale everything. "One aged man--one man--can't fill a house" sounds like a verdict, the repetition stripping him down to a single "one." Then the list widens to "A farm, a countryside," and the hedge "or if he can" reopens the question. "It's thus he does it of a winter night" points back to everything we have watched: the forgetting, the clomping, the fading light, the sleep. That is the filling. It is hollow, like the box, but it is real, because no one else is there to do it. The poem ends in neither pity nor celebration but in a grudging respect for presence at its smallest.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis must make a claim about how the poem presents the old man's solitude, and it must go beyond saying the poem is 'about loneliness' or 'about old age.' Strong theses identify a tension, for example that the man is pitiably reduced (forgetful, dimming, outmatched by the night) yet also asserts a stubborn, limited power to keep house against the dark, or that the final lines turn pity into qualified respect. A thesis that only lists devices ('Frost uses imagery and personification'), only restates the prompt, or makes a claim the text cannot support (for example that the man definitely dies in the poem, or that the poem is simply celebratory) does not earn the point. The thesis may be more than one sentence and may appear anywhere, but it must be identifiable.

Strong responses (3-4 points) select specific evidence from across the poem and explain how it builds the divided view: the personified night that 'looked darkly in at him' and the gaze he cannot return; the convoluted syntax of 'What kept him from remembering what it was' that enacts his confusion; the caesura in 'at a loss'; the comic-pathetic 'clomping' and the simile 'like beating on a box' that make his noise both intrusive and absurd against the night's 'common things'; the shrinking repetition of 'A light he was to no one but himself' and 'A quiet light, and then not even that'; the possessives 'his snow' and 'His icicles' entrusted to the 'broken moon'; and the concluding qualified claim 'can't fill a house... or if he can.' Commentary must connect each choice to the line of reasoning (how it shows diminishment, how it shows persistence or ownership, or how the two interact) rather than labeling devices or paraphrasing. A 2 typically offers accurate but general commentary or focuses only on loneliness and decay; a 1 mostly summarizes the old man's actions; a 0 is off-topic or mere restatement. Responses that track the movement of the poem, from the man as observed object to the final assertion, generally reason more effectively than device-by-device lists.

Sophistication may be earned by exploring the poem's complexity, for example by showing how the last three lines rescale the poem (house, farm, countryside) and recast everything before them, so that 'thus he does it' names both a hollow, fragile filling and a real one; by analyzing how the speaker's tone balances pity with dry humor (the scared cellar, the box) without mocking him; by examining the ambiguity of the light going out and the man sleeping 'still,' noting how the poem gestures toward death without stating it; or by considering how the 'broken moon' as a fitting keeper mirrors the man's own brokenness. Writing that is especially vivid and controlled in service of such an argument can also qualify. A single sweeping statement or an unsupported claim about Frost's life or rural America does not earn the point.

Sample essay (mid; scored 4/6: thesis 1, evidence 3, sophistication 0)
In "An Old Man's Winter Night," Robert Frost presents an old man who is weak, forgetful, and small compared to the huge cold night outside, but who still manages, in a small way, to hold onto his house. The poem pities him, yet by the end it also gives him a kind of quiet dignity, and Frost shows both through imagery, sound, and the way the poem ends.

At the start the man is shown as someone being watched instead of someone acting. "All out of doors looked darkly in at him" makes the night into a person who stares at the house, and the old man cannot stare back because "the lamp tilted near them in his hand" blocks his eyes. This makes him seem weak, since he is outmatched by the dark and does not even see how big it is. His forgetfulness is also shown by the sentence "What kept him from remembering what it was." The sentence is long and twisting, so the reader gets a little lost like he does, and the line "He stood with barrels round him--at a loss" stops with a dash to show him stuck in the cellar. The barrels surround him and make him look small.

Frost also uses sound to make him seem both silly and sad. The word "clomping" is heavy and clumsy, and the poem says he "scared the cellar under him." This is almost funny, since the cellar is scared of an old man, but it also shows how his noise is out of place. The night has "common things" like the roar of trees, and compared to that his noise is "like beating on a box." The simile makes him sound hollow and small, like he is only banging on something empty.

The poem then gets quieter. "A light he was to no one but himself" and then "A quiet light, and then not even that" shrink him step by step until the light seems to go out, which could hint at death, though he is really just asleep. Still, the man does not disappear. He gives his "snow" and "icicles" to the moon to keep, and the words "his" and "His" show he thinks of them as belonging to him. The "broken moon" is a fitting guard because it is damaged like he is.

The last lines say "One aged man--one man--can't fill a house," but then add "or if he can, / It's thus he does it of a winter night." The repetition of "one man" stresses how little he is, but the "or if he can" lets in a doubt. In the end Frost suggests that the old man fills the place only barely, by being there, sleeping and breathing in the cold, and that this is small but still real.

It is somewhat general and the final 'how' is only a list of devices.
- Row B: "makes the night into a person who stares at the house" - Correctly identifies personification and links it to the man's weakness, but the explanation stays brief and does not develop how the unreturned gaze shapes the poem's view.
- Row B: "The sentence is long and twisting, so the reader gets a little lost like he does" - Good attempt to connect syntax to his confusion, a specific technique tied to the argument, though the commentary is thin and a bit informal.
- Row B: "The simile makes him sound hollow and small, like he is only banging on something empty." - Specific evidence with commentary on the simile's effect, but the essay does not connect it to the 'common things' contrast or to the man's persistence, so the reasoning stays one-sided here.

- Row C: "the "or if he can" lets in a doubt" - Touches on the qualified final claim and gives a modest reading; the conclusion mostly restates the thesis and does not explore how the ending reframes the whole poem, so it does not reach sophistication.

In "An Old Man's Winter Night" Robert Frost writes about an old man who is alone in his house on a cold winter night. The poem shows that being old and alone is sad and hard, and Frost uses imagery and personification to show this.

The poem starts with the outside world looking in at the old man. It says "All out of doors looked darkly in at him" which makes the night seem like a person watching him. The frost is on the window and the stars are shining through it. This makes the old man seem small because the night is so big and he is just in a house. Then he goes down to the cellar with a lamp and he forgets why he went there. The poem says he stood "with barrels round him--at a loss." So he is old and forgetful and cannot remember things.

Next the poem says he "scared the cellar" by clomping around. This shows he is loud and clumsy. The noise he makes is compared to "beating on a box." Then he sits down and the poem says he is "a light" to no one but himself. This means he is lonely because nobody else is there to see him. The light also goes out, so it is sad.

Then the old man falls asleep by the stove and a log shifts and he moves a little but keeps sleeping. The poem ends by saying one man cannot fill a house, a farm, or a countryside. This shows that the man is very alone and that the house is too big for him. In conclusion, Frost shows that the old man is lonely and old, and the poem is sad because he is by himself on a winter night.

The poem moves from pity toward qualified respect: though frail and forgetful, the man claims ownership ('his snow,' 'His icicles') and, through his mere presence and noise, holds the house against the night in the only way one person can.
The speaker balances pathos with gentle humor, so that the man's clomping and box-like noise seem both absurd and touching, keeping the poem from either sentimentality or mockery.
The poem uses sleep and the fading light to gesture toward death, so that the man's keeping of the house is shown as precarious and temporary even as it is affirmed.
The poem contrasts the vast, indifferent natural world (night, trees, broken moon) with the small human presence, suggesting that human meaning is limited and fragile but still real.

devices.quote: All out of doors looked darkly in at him
devices.effect: Makes the night a watching presence pressing in on the house, casting the man as observed and exposed, and setting up the contest between his small presence and the vast outside.

devices.quote: Through the thin frost, almost in separate stars,
devices.effect: The frost on the window looks like a cold, distant sky, fusing the windowpane with the cosmos and stressing how thin the barrier is between the man and the emptiness outside.

devices.quote: That brought him to that creaking room was age.
devices.effect: The long, winding sentence holds back its subject until the last word, 'age,' acting out the man's lapse of memory and landing on the cause flatly.

devices.quote: He stood with barrels round him--at a loss.
devices.effect: The dash forces a pause that copies his stalled confusion, leaving him stranded among the objects of the cellar.

devices.quote: he scared it once again
devices.effect: The repeated 'scared' and 'clomping' give his movement a clumsy, slightly comic insistence, so his noise is the way he asserts himself, however awkwardly.

devices.quote: But nothing so like beating on a box.
devices.effect: Sets the man's hollow, unnatural sound apart from the night's 'common things,' making him both intrusive and pitiably small, a noise the natural world does not recognize.

devices.quote: A quiet light, and then not even that.
devices.effect: Picking up 'A light he was to no one but himself,' the repeated and shrinking light traces his fading presence, literally the lamp going out and figuratively a hint of mortality.

devices.quote: to the broken moon
devices.effect: Entrusting his house to a damaged, 'late-arising' moon pictures a guardian as worn as he is, a fitting but uncertain stand-in for his watchfulness.

devices.quote: His icicles along the wall to keep;
devices.effect: The possessive 'His' (echoing 'his snow') claims ownership even over winter's cold, suggesting dignity and stubborn stewardship in the middle of decline.

devices.quote: One aged man--one man--can't fill a house,
devices.effect: The halting self-correction and plain denial make the closing claim modest, and so the qualified turn that follows feels earned rather than sentimental.

devices.quote: It's thus he does it of a winter night.
devices.effect: The closing line turns the poem's pity into a wry, qualified affirmation, recasting all his fumbling, noise, and sleep as the way a single life fills a place.

common_pitfalls: Summarizing the old man's actions in order without explaining how the language shapes our view of him.
Stating as fact that the old man dies, ignoring 'but still slept,' instead of treating the death imagery as suggestion or ambiguity.
Reading the poem as only sad or only uplifting, and so missing the tension the final lines create.
Listing devices (personification, imagery, repetition) without tying them to a claim about solitude, diminishment, or presence.
Bringing in unsupported biographical claims about Frost or general claims about rural life in place of textual evidence.
Ignoring the final three lines, which change the meaning of the whole poem.

samples.essay:
Frost's old man is easy to pity. He forgets why he went to the cellar, he cannot meet the stare of the night, and by the end even his lamp is gone. But the poem does not let pity have the last word. Through personification, tangled syntax, and shrinking repetition, Frost shows a man reduced almost to nothing. Yet through possessive language and a final hedged statement, he insists that this reduced man still holds his house against the dark, and that holding it this way, half-asleep and barely visible, may be the only way anyone could.

The opening makes the man an object instead of an observer. "All out of doors looked darkly in at him" turns the whole winter world into a watcher, and the lamp "tilted near" his eyes keeps him from "giving back the gaze." The light that should help him see actually blinds him to what is outside, so from the first lines his one defense against the dark is also what isolates him. Frost then lets the sentence structure act out his confusion. "What kept him from remembering what it was" circles through two "what" clauses before it finally lands on "age," so the reader, like the man, has to grope for the point. When the line arrives at "at a loss," the dash before it works like a stall in his thinking, a blank where his purpose should be.

What makes this more than a portrait of decline is the speaker's dry humor. The man "scared the cellar under him / In clomping there," then scared it "once again" on the way out. "Clomping" is a clumsy, almost cartoonish word, and frightening a cellar is funny. But the joke turns when he scares "the outer night" too. The night knows the "roar / Of trees and crack of branches, common things," yet has heard nothing "so like beating on a box." The simile deflates him and is oddly proud of him at once: his noise is a hollow knocking, but it is also unlike anything in nature. For a moment the vast night is the one startled. Frost lets us laugh at the man without mocking him, because the small noise really does register.

The middle of the poem shrinks him through repetition. "A light he was to no one but himself" already narrows his reach, and "A quiet light, and then not even that" erases it. The word "light" dims every time it comes back. Read alone, this sounds like death, and the poem seems to lean that way. But Frost pulls back: the man "slept," shifts when a log jolts in the stove, and "still slept." "Still" means both motionless and continuing, so the poem gestures toward death while keeping him alive.

Even asleep, he claims ownership. He hands "his snow upon the roof, / His icicles along the wall" to the moon to keep. The possessives are stubborn, since snow and ice belong to no one, yet he treats them as property under his watch. His chosen keeper is "the broken moon," late and partial, "As better than the sun." A broken guardian fits a broken man, and his choice suggests he understands that diminished things can still do a job.

The last three lines rescale everything. "One aged man--one man--can't fill a house" sounds like a verdict, the repetition stripping him down to a single "one." Then the list widens to "A farm, a countryside," and the hedge "or if he can" reopens the question. "It's thus he does it of a winter night" points back to everything we have watched: the forgetting, the clomping, the fading light, the sleep. That is the filling. It is hollow, like the box, but it is real, because no one else is there to do it. The poem ends in neither pity nor celebration but in a grudging respect for presence at its smallest.

In "An Old Man's Winter Night," Robert Frost presents an old man who is weak, forgetful, and small compared to the huge cold night outside, but who still manages, in a small way, to hold onto his house. The poem pities him, yet by the end it also gives him a kind of quiet dignity, and Frost shows both through imagery, sound, and the way the poem ends.

At the start the man is shown as someone being watched instead of someone acting. "All out of doors looked darkly in at him" makes the night into a person who stares at the house, and the old man cannot stare back because "the lamp tilted near them in his hand" blocks his eyes. This makes him seem weak, since he is outmatched by the dark and does not even see how big it is. His forgetfulness is also shown by the sentence "What kept him from remembering what it was." The sentence is long and twisting, so the reader gets a little lost like he does, and the line "He stood with barrels round him--at a loss" stops with a dash to show him stuck in the cellar. The barrels surround him and make him look small.

Frost also uses sound to make him seem both silly and sad. The word "clomping" is heavy and clumsy, and the poem says he "scared the cellar under him." This is almost funny, since the cellar is scared of an old man, but it also shows how his noise is out of place. The night has "common things" like the roar of trees, and compared to that his noise is "like beating on a box." The simile makes him sound hollow and small, like he is only banging on something empty.

The poem then gets quieter. "A light he was to no one but himself" and then "A quiet light, and then not even that" shrink him step by step until the light seems to go out, which could hint at death, though he is really just asleep. Still, the man does not disappear. He gives his "snow" and "icicles" to the moon to keep, and the words "his" and "His" show he thinks of them as belonging to him. The "broken moon" is a fitting guard because it is damaged like he is.

The last lines say "One aged man--one man--can't fill a house," but then add "or if he can, / It's thus he does it of a winter night." The repetition of "one man" stresses how little he is, but the "or if he can" lets in a doubt. In the end Frost suggests that the old man fills the place only barely, by being there, sleeping and breathing in the cold, and that this is small but still real.

```passage
    Mr. Ryder might aptly be called the dean of the Blue
Veins. The original Blue Veins were a little society of
colored persons organized in a certain Northern city
shortly after the war. Its purpose was to establish and
maintain correct social standards among a people whose
social condition presented almost unlimited room for
improvement. By accident, combined perhaps with some
natural affinity, the society consisted of individuals
who were, generally speaking, more white than black.
Some envious outsider made the suggestion that no one
was eligible for membership who was not white enough to
show blue veins. The suggestion was readily adopted by
those who were not of the favored few, and since that
time the society, though possessing a longer and more
pretentious name, had been known far and wide as the
"Blue Vein Society," and its members as the "Blue
Veins."

    The Blue Veins did not allow that any such
requirement existed for admission to their circle, but,
on the contrary, declared that character and culture
were the only things considered; and that if most of
their members were light-colored, it was because such
persons, as a rule, had had better opportunities to
qualify themselves for membership. Opinions differed,
too, as to the usefulness of the society. There were
those who had been known to assail it violently as a
glaring example of the very prejudice from which the
colored race had suffered most; and later, when such
critics had succeeded in getting on the inside, they had
been heard to maintain with zeal and earnestness that
the society was a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a
shield,--a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night,
to guide their people through the social wilderness.
Another alleged prerequisite for Blue Vein membership
was that of free birth; and while there was really no
such requirement, it is doubtless true that very few of
the members would have been unable to meet it if there
had been. If there were one or two of the older members
who had come up from the South and from slavery, their
history presented enough romantic circumstances to rob
their servile origin of its grosser aspects.

    While there were no such tests of eligibility, it is
true that the Blue Veins had their notions on these
subjects, and that not all of them were equally liberal
in regard to the things they collectively disclaimed.
Mr. Ryder was one of the most conservative. Though he
had not been among the founders of the society, but had
come in some years later, his genius for social
leadership was such that he had speedily become its
recognized adviser and head, the custodian of its
standards, and the preserver of its traditions. He
shaped its social policy, was active in providing for
its entertainment, and when the interest fell off, as it
sometimes did, he fanned the embers until they burst
again into a cheerful flame.

    There were still other reasons for his popularity.
While he was not as white as some of the Blue Veins, his
appearance was such as to confer distinction upon them.
His features were of a refined type, his hair was almost
straight; he was always neatly dressed; his manners were
irreproachable, and his morals above suspicion. He had
come to Groveland a young man, and obtaining employment
in the office of a railroad company as messenger had in
time worked himself up to the position of stationery
clerk, having charge of the distribution of the office
supplies for the whole company. Although the lack of
early training had hindered the orderly development of a
naturally fine mind, it had not prevented him from doing
a great deal of reading or from forming decidedly
literary tastes. Poetry was his passion. He could repeat
whole pages of the great English poets; and if his
pronunciation was sometimes faulty, his eye, his voice,
his gestures, would respond to the changing sentiment
with a precision that revealed a poetic soul and
disarmed criticism. He was economical, and had saved
money; he owned and occupied a very comfortable house on
a respectable street. His residence was handsomely
furnished, containing among other things a good library,
especially rich in poetry, a piano, and some choice
engravings. He generally shared his house with some
young couple, who looked after his wants and were
company for him; for Mr. Ryder was a single man. In the
early days of his connection with the Blue Veins he had
been regarded as quite a catch, and young ladies and
their mothers had manoeuvred with much ingenuity to
capture him. Not, however, until Mrs. Molly Dixon
visited Groveland had any woman ever made him wish to
change his condition to that of a married man.
```

parts.prompt:
The following passage is from "The Wife of His Youth," a short story by Charles W. Chesnutt (1899 in the original). In this passage, the narrator describes the "Blue Vein Society," a social club of mostly light-skinned colored people founded in a Northern city shortly after the war, and introduces Mr. Ryder, its leading member.

Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Charles W. Chesnutt uses literary elements and techniques to convey the narrator's divided attitude toward the Blue Veins and Mr. Ryder, a measured respect for their ambition, refinement, and self-made success alongside quiet irony about the color and class prejudice they officially deny.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the passage.
- Use specific evidence from the passage, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple literary elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
In the opening of "The Wife of His Youth," Chesnutt's narrator sounds a lot like a member of the club he is describing. He is courteous and measured, and he never quite accuses anyone of anything. That politeness is the joke. Through hedging syntax, denials that end up confirming what they deny, and a portrait of Mr. Ryder built out of concessions and inventories, the narrator gives the Blue Veins real credit for their ambition and refinement while letting their color prejudice show through the gaps in their own explanations. The irony stays quiet because it borrows the society's genteel manner, so the style ends up taking part in the respectability it questions.

The narrator's treatment of the society as a group depends on qualifiers. The members are light-skinned "By accident, combined perhaps with some natural affinity," a phrase that pretends to be neutral but slips. "By accident" and "perhaps" sound fair-minded, but "natural affinity" suggests that lightness is something the members are drawn to, a preference and not a coincidence. The nickname comes from "some envious outsider," which seems to dismiss it, yet it was "readily adopted," and a joke only spreads that fast if people think it is accurate. The society's official claim, that "character and culture were the only things considered," comes to us in indirect speech, so the narrator reports it without standing behind it. Still, he is not just mocking. The excuse that light-skinned people had "better opportunities" is partly true, given slavery's history, and the narrator lets it be both a plausible point and a convenient one.

The irony is sharpest with the critics who change sides once they get "on the inside." Their praise piles up into "a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a shield," and the list is inflated past the point of meaning anything. Then the scriptural "pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night" turns a social club into the guide that led Israel out of Egypt. This exaggeration exposes how quickly principle gives way to belonging. But "the social wilderness" is not a totally empty phrase, because freed people after the war really were in an unfamiliar world. So the satire is aimed at the converts' zeal and not at the need the society answers. The same doubleness shows up in the sentence about free birth: "while there was really no such requirement, it is doubtless true" that few "would have been unable to meet it." The double negative and the long, winding clauses copy the society's own evasions. Even slavery gets edited, since "romantic circumstances" serve to "rob their servile origin of its grosser aspects." Painful history is rewritten as respectable romance, and the narrator's mild word "grosser" makes the cover-up sound like good taste.

Mr. Ryder gets a warmer but still ironic portrait. The language of office, "custodian of its standards, and the preserver of its traditions," honors his leadership, and the image of him fanning "the embers until they burst again into a cheerful flame" is honestly affectionate. Yet just before this the narrator calls him "one of the most conservative" about "the things they collectively disclaimed," so the standards he guards include the prejudice the group denies. The list of his traits makes this concrete: "his hair was almost straight" sits in the same series as "his morals above suspicion," and the parallel syntax treats nearness to whiteness as if it were a virtue. The word "almost" measures him on the same scale the society pretends it doesn't use. His rise from messenger to stationery clerk is real self-made success, though the grand phrasing about supplies "for the whole company" gently deflates it. The concession "if his pronunciation was sometimes faulty" leads into a soul that "disarmed criticism," and the narrator seems disarmed too. Even his "very comfortable house on a respectable street," with its piano and engravings, measures worth in objects.

The last sentence turns from public standards to private desire, as Molly Dixon makes Ryder want to "change his condition." That word echoes the "social condition" the society was founded to improve. It hints that Ryder's carefully guarded standards are about to meet his personal life, and that the narrator's balance of respect and irony is going to be tested along with them.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis must make an interpretive claim about the narrator's attitude toward the Blue Veins and/or Mr. Ryder that goes beyond summary. Strong theses name the doubleness, for example that the narrator's polite, judicious voice both honors the society's aims and Ryder's achievements and exposes the color prejudice hidden under its claims of 'character and culture.' A thesis that only says the society is light-skinned, or that the narrator 'describes Mr. Ryder,' does not earn the point. A thesis that reads the passage as purely admiring or as open, bitter condemnation can earn the point only if it is defensible and argued, but such one-sided readings usually limit performance in Row B. Restating the prompt or just listing devices ('the author uses irony and imagery') does not count.

Strong responses look closely at how the narrator's careful, hedging syntax produces the irony: the denials that admit what they deny ('while there was really no such requirement, it is doubtless true that very few of the members would have been unable to meet it'), the outsider's joke about blue veins being 'readily adopted,' and the critics who change their minds once 'on the inside' and then pile up inflated metaphors ('a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a shield') and the scriptural 'pillar of cloud.' For Ryder, responses should analyze the list of physical traits that ties his 'distinction' to whiteness ('his hair was almost straight'), the concessive sentences that admit a flaw and then praise him ('if his pronunciation was sometimes faulty'), the language of office and guardianship ('custodian of its standards'), and the details of possessions that measure respectability. Commentary has to explain how these choices create both respect and irony, not just point to them. For a 4, the response should trace the attitude across the passage, from the society's group self-deception to the more sympathetic yet still ironic portrait of Ryder, and might note the closing turn toward Mrs. Molly Dixon. A 3 explains relevant evidence with some uneven commentary. A 2 mostly summarizes or names devices with thin explanation. A 1 gives general or inaccurate claims.

Sophistication can be earned by working through the tension rather than settling it. Examples: arguing that the narrator's own genteel, Blue-Vein-like politeness is the tool of the satire, so the style takes part in what it mocks; explaining how Ryder can be both admirably self-made and complicit in the hierarchy he guards ('one of the most conservative'); seeing that the slavery passage ('rob their servile origin of its grosser aspects') shows the society reshaping painful history into respectable romance; or reading the final sentence about Mrs. Molly Dixon as a sign that personal desire will test Ryder's standards. The insight must run through the argument. A single complex-sounding sentence or speculation about the rest of the story without textual grounding does not earn the point.

Sample essay (high; scored 6/6: thesis 1, evidence 4, sophistication 1)
In the opening of "The Wife of His Youth," Chesnutt's narrator sounds a lot like a member of the club he is describing. He is courteous and measured, and he never quite accuses anyone of anything. That politeness is the joke. Through hedging syntax, denials that end up confirming what they deny, and a portrait of Mr. Ryder built out of concessions and inventories, the narrator gives the Blue Veins real credit for their ambition and refinement while letting their color prejudice show through the gaps in their own explanations. The irony stays quiet because it borrows the society's genteel manner, so the style ends up taking part in the respectability it questions.

The narrator's treatment of the society as a group depends on qualifiers. The members are light-skinned "By accident, combined perhaps with some natural affinity," a phrase that pretends to be neutral but slips. "By accident" and "perhaps" sound fair-minded, but "natural affinity" suggests that lightness is something the members are drawn to, a preference and not a coincidence. The nickname comes from "some envious outsider," which seems to dismiss it, yet it was "readily adopted," and a joke only spreads that fast if people think it is accurate. The society's official claim, that "character and culture were the only things considered," comes to us in indirect speech, so the narrator reports it without standing behind it. Still, he is not just mocking. The excuse that light-skinned people had "better opportunities" is partly true, given slavery's history, and the narrator lets it be both a plausible point and a convenient one.

The irony is sharpest with the critics who change sides once they get "on the inside." Their praise piles up into "a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a shield," and the list is inflated past the point of meaning anything. Then the scriptural "pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night" turns a social club into the guide that led Israel out of Egypt. This exaggeration exposes how quickly principle gives way to belonging. But "the social wilderness" is not a totally empty phrase, because freed people after the war really were in an unfamiliar world. So the satire is aimed at the converts' zeal and not at the need the society answers. The same doubleness shows up in the sentence about free birth: "while there was really no such requirement, it is doubtless true" that few "would have been unable to meet it." The double negative and the long, winding clauses copy the society's own evasions. Even slavery gets edited, since "romantic circumstances" serve to "rob their servile origin of its grosser aspects." Painful history is rewritten as respectable romance, and the narrator's mild word "grosser" makes the cover-up sound like good taste.

Mr. Ryder gets a warmer but still ironic portrait. The language of office, "custodian of its standards, and the preserver of its traditions," honors his leadership, and the image of him fanning "the embers until they burst again into a cheerful flame" is honestly affectionate. Yet just before this the narrator calls him "one of the most conservative" about "the things they collectively disclaimed," so the standards he guards include the prejudice the group denies. The list of his traits makes this concrete: "his hair was almost straight" sits in the same series as "his morals above suspicion," and the parallel syntax treats nearness to whiteness as if it were a virtue. The word "almost" measures him on the same scale the society pretends it doesn't use. His rise from messenger to stationery clerk is real self-made success, though the grand phrasing about supplies "for the whole company" gently deflates it. The concession "if his pronunciation was sometimes faulty" leads into a soul that "disarmed criticism," and the narrator seems disarmed too. Even his "very comfortable house on a respectable street," with its piano and engravings, measures worth in objects.

The last sentence turns from public standards to private desire, as Molly Dixon makes Ryder want to "change his condition." That word echoes the "social condition" the society was founded to improve. It hints that Ryder's carefully guarded standards are about to meet his personal life, and that the narrator's balance of respect and irony is going to be tested along with them.

In this passage from "The Wife of His Youth," Charles Chesnutt's narrator describes the Blue Vein Society and Mr. Ryder with a tone that is respectful on the surface but quietly ironic underneath. The narrator admires the ambition and self-improvement of these people, but he also shows, through careful wording, that their claims about "character and culture" hide a prejudice about color and class that they will not admit.

The irony is clearest in how the narrator describes the society's rules. The society "did not allow that any such requirement existed," yet the narrator notes that most members were "more white than black." The narrator never directly accuses them, but by putting the denial next to the fact, the reader sees the contradiction. The same thing happens with free birth. The narrator says "there was really no such requirement," and then adds that "very few of the members" would have failed it anyway. The hedging words like "doubtless" and "generally speaking" make the narrator sound polite and fair, but they actually admit the thing the Blue Veins deny. The narrator also uses the critics who first attacked the society as "prejudice" and then, once inside, called it "a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a shield." The long list of metaphors is exaggerated, and the biblical "pillar of cloud" makes the society sound almost holy. This shows the narrator smiling at how people change their opinion when they benefit.

Toward Mr. Ryder the tone is warmer, though still not simple. lit_frq.title: Prose Fiction Analysis: The Wife of His Youth

prompt.lead: The following passage is from "The Wife of His Youth," a short story by Charles W. Chesnutt (1899 in the original). In this passage, the narrator describes the "Blue Vein Society," a social club of mostly light-skinned colored people founded in a Northern city shortly after the war, and introduces Mr. Ryder, its leading member.
prompt.task: Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Charles W. Chesnutt uses literary elements and techniques to convey the narrator's divided attitude toward the Blue Veins and Mr. Ryder, a measured respect for their ambition, refinement, and self-made success alongside quiet irony about the color and class prejudice they officially deny.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the passage.
Use specific evidence from the passage, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
Explain how multiple literary elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

passage.title: The Wife of His Youth
passage.headnote: The following passage from a short story is by Charles W. Chesnutt (1899). This is an excerpt.
stanzas: Mr. Ryder might aptly be called the dean of the Blue
Veins. The original Blue Veins were a little society of
colored persons organized in a certain Northern city
shortly after the war. Its purpose was to establish and
maintain correct social standards among a people whose
social condition presented almost unlimited room for
improvement. By accident, combined perhaps with some
natural affinity, the society consisted of individuals
who were, generally speaking, more white than black.
Some envious outsider made the suggestion that no one
was eligible for membership who was not white enough to
show blue veins. The suggestion was readily adopted by
those who were not of the favored few, and since that
time the society, though possessing a longer and more
pretentious name, had been known far and wide as the
"Blue Vein Society," and its members as the "Blue
Veins."
The Blue Veins did not allow that any such
requirement existed for admission to their circle, but,
on the contrary, declared that character and culture
were the only things considered; and that if most of
their members were light-colored, it was because such
persons, as a rule, had had better opportunities to
qualify themselves for membership. Opinions differed,
too, as to the usefulness of the society. There were
those who had been known to assail it violently as a
glaring example of the very prejudice from which the
colored race had suffered most; and later, when such
critics had succeeded in getting on the inside, they had
been heard to maintain with zeal and earnestness that
the society was a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a
shield,--a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night,
to guide their people through the social wilderness.
Another alleged prerequisite for Blue Vein membership
was that of free birth; and while there was really no
such requirement, it is doubtless true that very few of
the members would have been unable to meet it if there
had been. If there were one or two of the older members
who had come up from the South and from slavery, their
history presented enough romantic circumstances to rob
their servile origin of its grosser aspects.
While there were no such tests of eligibility, it is
true that the Blue Veins had their notions on these
subjects, and that not all of them were equally liberal
in regard to the things they collectively disclaimed.
Mr. Ryder was one of the most conservative. Though he
had not been among the founders of the society, but had
come in some years later, his genius for social
leadership was such that he had speedily become its
recognized adviser and head, the custodian of its
standards, and the preserver of its traditions. He
shaped its social policy, was active in providing for
its entertainment, and when the interest fell off, as it
sometimes did, he fanned the embers until they burst
again into a cheerful flame.
There were still other reasons for his popularity.
While he was not as white as some of the Blue Veins, his
appearance was such as to confer distinction upon them.
His features were of a refined type, his hair was almost
straight; he was always neatly dressed; his manners were
irreproachable, and his morals above suspicion. He had
come to Groveland a young man, and obtaining employment
in the office of a railroad company as messenger had in
time worked himself up to the position of stationery
clerk, having charge of the distribution of the office
supplies for the whole company. Although the lack of
early training had hindered the orderly development of a
naturally fine mind, it had not prevented him from doing
a great deal of reading or from forming decidedly
literary tastes. Poetry was his passion. He could repeat
whole pages of the great English poets; and if his
pronunciation was sometimes faulty, his eye, his voice,
his gestures, would respond to the changing sentiment
with a precision that revealed a poetic soul and
disarmed criticism. He was economical, and had saved
money; he owned and occupied a very comfortable house on
a respectable street. His residence was handsomely
furnished, containing among other things a good library,
especially rich in poetry, a piano, and some choice
engravings. He generally shared his house with some
young couple, who looked after his wants and were
company for him; for Mr. Ryder was a single man. In the
early days of his connection with the Blue Veins he had
been regarded as quite a catch, and young ladies and
their mothers had manoeuvred with much ingenuity to
capture him. Not, however, until Mrs. Molly Dixon
visited Groveland had any woman ever made him wish to
change his condition to that of a married man.

Listing devices (irony, metaphor, allusion) without explaining how they shape the narrator's divided attitude.
Summarizing Ryder's biography and possessions without analyzing what the details suggest about respectability and race.

Missing the shift in the passage from the collective satire of the society to the individual, more sympathetic portrait of Ryder.

The word "almost" measures him on the same scale the society pretends it doesn't use. His rise from messenger to stationery clerk is real self-made success, though the grand phrasing about supplies "for the whole company" gently deflates it. The concession "if his pronunciation was sometimes faulty" leads into a soul that "disarmed criticism," and the narrator seems disarmed too. Even his "very comfortable house on a respectable street," with its piano and engravings, measures worth in objects.

The last sentence turns from public standards to private desire, as Molly Dixon makes Ryder want to "change his condition." That word echoes the "social condition" the society was founded to improve. It hints that Ryder's carefully guarded standards are about to meet his personal life, and that the narrator's balance of respect and irony is going to be tested along with them.

samples.essay:
In this passage from "The Wife of His Youth," Charles Chesnutt's narrator describes the Blue Vein Society and Mr. Ryder with a tone that is respectful on the surface but quietly ironic underneath. The narrator admires the ambition and self-improvement of these people, but he also shows, through careful wording, that their claims about "character and culture" hide a prejudice about color and class that they will not admit.

The irony is clearest in how the narrator describes the society's rules. The society "did not allow that any such requirement existed," yet the narrator notes that most members were "more white than black." The narrator never directly accuses them, but by putting the denial next to the fact, the reader sees the contradiction. The same thing happens with free birth. The narrator says "there was really no such requirement," and then adds that "very few of the members" would have failed it anyway. The hedging words like "doubtless" and "generally speaking" make the narrator sound polite and fair, but they actually admit the thing the Blue Veins deny. The narrator also uses the critics who first attacked the society as "prejudice" and then, once inside, called it "a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a shield." The long list of metaphors is exaggerated, and the biblical "pillar of cloud" makes the society sound almost holy. This shows the narrator smiling at how people change their opinion when they benefit.

Toward Mr. Ryder the tone is warmer, though still not simple. The narrator gives a lot of specific detail about his success: he rose from messenger to stationery clerk, saved money, owned a "comfortable house," and had a library and a piano. These details show real respect, because Ryder worked for what he has. The sentence about his poetry is a good example of the mixed attitude. His "pronunciation was sometimes faulty," but his gestures "disarmed criticism." The narrator admits a flaw and then forgives it, which suggests sympathy for Ryder's sincere love of poetry. However, the narrator also says Ryder's appearance "confer[s] distinction" on the Blue Veins and mentions that "his hair was almost straight." Here Ryder's value to the society is tied to how close he is to white, which brings the irony back in. Calling him "dean" and "custodian of its standards" also makes him sound like an official guarding something, and the narrator says he was "one of the most conservative."

The passage ends by turning to Mrs. Molly Dixon, which hints that Ryder's life is not as controlled as he thinks. Overall, the narrator respects the Blue Veins and Ryder for their effort, but uses polite, hedged language to show that their standards are less open than they say.

In this passage Charles Chesnutt describes the Blue Vein Society and Mr. Ryder. The narrator talks about how the society started and what kind of people were in it, and then he describes Mr. Ryder who is the leader. The narrator seems to respect them but also finds some things funny about them, and Chesnutt uses different literary techniques to show this.

At the start the narrator explains that the society was organized "shortly after the war" to set up "correct social standards." This shows the society had a good purpose because the people needed improvement. But then the narrator says that the members were "more white than black," which shows that the society was really about color. The Blue Veins say that "character and culture" were the only things considered, but the narrator does not seem to believe this. He uses a kind of irony because he says one thing but the reader knows it is different.

Later the narrator talks about critics who attacked the society and then got in and called it "a lifeboat, an anchor, a bulwark and a shield." This is a list which is exaggerated and it makes the critics seem like hypocrites. The narrator is making fun of them a little.

When the narrator describes Mr. Ryder he is mostly positive. Ryder worked his way up from messenger to stationery clerk, and he reads poetry and owns a nice house. These details show he is a hard worker and self-made. The narrator says "his hair was almost straight" which shows that looks matter to the Blue Veins too. Ryder is also called "one of the most conservative" so he is strict about the rules.

In conclusion, Chesnutt uses irony, lists, and details about Ryder to show that the narrator respects the Blue Veins but also sees their prejudice. The passage ends with Mrs. Molly Dixon, which sets up the rest of the story.

blueprint.central_idea: Through a courteous, measured narrative voice, the passage both honors and gently satirizes a post-war society of light-skinned colored people and its leader, Mr. Ryder: it respects their ambition and self-made refinement while exposing, through hedged denials and inflated praise, the color and class prejudice they officially disclaim.
blueprint.complexity: The irony works through restraint, not open attack. The narrator borrows the society's own genteel style to show its contradictions, and the respect for Ryder is real even as his distinction is tied to near-white features and guarding exclusive standards. Students have to hold sympathy and critique together, notice the shift from group satire to individual portrait, and see how the ending turns toward personal desire.
